- If sentiment is positive (≥ 0.3) and forecast is rising steadily, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment is negative (≤ -0.3) and forecast is falling, avoid excessive downward bias — consider slight upward correction.  
- After a sharp price spike, model tends to overcorrect downward — apply a “lagged overshoot” rule: if last 3–5 days show high volatility, reduce forecast by 2–5% to account for mean reversion.  
- When sentiment is neutral (0.0–0.2) and price is trending, model often underestimates upside — increase forecast by 1–3% for next 3–5 days.  
- If true outcome deviates >5% from forecast in first 3–5 days, adjust future forecast to align with recent history — especially if sentiment is volatile.  
- For 30-day horizon, if forecast is flat or slowly rising while true outcome shows strong divergence, consider “sentiment-driven drift” — if sentiment is positive, add 0.5–1.5% to forecast; if negative, subtract 0.5–1.5%.
